$$
x=\{23,\,21,\,25\},\,y=\{10,\,8,\,9\}
$$

You're given that $\overset{―}{x}=23,$ $\overset{―}{y}=9,$ ${\sigma }_{x}≈1.633,$ and ${\sigma }_{y}≈0.816.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(23-23)(10-9)+(21-23)(8-9)+(25-23)(9-9)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(0)(1)+(-2)(-1)+(2)(0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & ≈0.667\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{0.667}{1.633\cdot 0.816} \\  & ≈0.50\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-02b295dd-b963-57b2-a571-57614a7d6b62"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$
{S}_{xx}=41,\,{S}_{xy}=-39,\,{S}_{yy}=61
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-39)}{\sqrt{41}\cdot \sqrt{61}} \\  & ≈-\frac{39}{6.403\,124\cdot 7.810\,250} \\  & ≈-0.78\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8529b028-3069-5aca-862e-01bc09be8701"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-8529b028-3069-5aca-862e-01bc09be8701" :answer-field/id #uuid "8529b028-3069-5aca-862e-01bc09be8701" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-39e0e51f-31ac-5155-8515-0e388c62fff3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-bd17caa6-972d-5ccd-b882-e9178d4ee21f" "answer-8a800801-9386-5b81-a40b-00038098eb6c" "answer-39e0e51f-31ac-5155-8515-0e388c62fff3" "answer-c15c2293-64f4-5914-a1bd-d8219b7ea7b7" "answer-5cce0b31-4bcb-572e-b042-e52b018d39b9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-bd17caa6-972d-5ccd-b882-e9178d4ee21f" :answer/id #uuid "bd17caa6-972d-5ccd-b882-e9178d4ee21f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho ≈-0.57" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a800801-9386-5b81-a40b-00038098eb6c" :answer/id #uuid "8a800801-9386-5b81-a40b-00038098eb6c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho ≈-0.69" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-39e0e51f-31ac-5155-8515-0e388c62fff3" :answer/id #uuid "39e0e51f-31ac-5155-8515-0e388c62fff3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho ≈-0.78" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c15c2293-64f4-5914-a1bd-d8219b7ea7b7" :answer/id #uuid "c15c2293-64f4-5914-a1bd-d8219b7ea7b7" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho ≈0.69" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5cce0b31-4bcb-572e-b042-e52b018d39b9" :answer/id #uuid "5cce0b31-4bcb-572e-b042-e52b018d39b9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho ≈0.78" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-02585424-6726-555e-b4dc-cd93537b87a1" :question/id #uuid "02585424-6726-555e-b4dc-cd93537b87a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-134448" :question/problem "The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.

Using the formula, we get

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(5-5)^{2}+(8-5)^{2}+(2-5)^{2} \\  & =0+9+9 \\  & =18 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(-1-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(5-2)^{2} \\  & =9+0+9 \\  & =18\end{aligned}

$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bce4a32c-46b5-57a1-9ab0-97e8c5d0e836"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bce4a32c-46b5-57a1-9ab0-97e8c5d0e836" :answer-field/id #uuid "bce4a32c-46b5-57a1-9ab0-97e8c5d0e836" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-c6783e59-5110-5183-8ab7-9fe21fa826d3" :answer-field/choices ["answer-4dfd1c2e-ea6f-5434-a4d9-c0b132425dc5" "answer-3aa92092-4369-5ff2-8cce-7258d56ad264" "answer-c6783e59-5110-5183-8ab7-9fe21fa826d3" "answer-74b331b0-c98a-5a41-94f1-cfd562c37a49" "answer-a0660bf7-cc1e-50a6-b15e-2bc59fd44ea8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4dfd1c2e-ea6f-5434-a4d9-c0b132425dc5" :answer/id #uuid "4dfd1c2e-ea6f-5434-a4d9-c0b132425dc5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho =-0.2" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3aa92092-4369-5ff2-8cce-7258d56ad264" :answer/id #uuid "3aa92092-4369-5ff2-8cce-7258d56ad264" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho =-0.25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c6783e59-5110-5183-8ab7-9fe21fa826d3" :answer/id #uuid "c6783e59-5110-5183-8ab7-9fe21fa826d3" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho =-0.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-74b331b0-c98a-5a41-94f1-cfd562c37a49" :answer/id #uuid "74b331b0-c98a-5a41-94f1-cfd562c37a49" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho =0.25" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a0660bf7-cc1e-50a6-b15e-2bc59fd44ea8" :answer/id #uuid "a0660bf7-cc1e-50a6-b15e-2bc59fd44ea8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\rho =0.5" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-aab6da21-f97b-5ce7-b157-a7c2c5069279" :question/id #uuid "aab6da21-f97b-5ce7-b157-a7c2c5069279" :question/math-academy-id "q-134404" :question/problem "An ergonomist investigates $4$ factories. He wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between $x,$ the money spent by factory owners on safety training courses, and $y,$ the number of accidents per year in the factories. The data is shown below.

| **Money spent (hundreds of $$$)** | **$10$** | **$15$** | **$12$** | **$23$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Number of accidents** | $3$ | $6$ | $5$ | $2$ |

You are given that the means are $\overset{―}{x}=15$ and $\overset{―}{y}=4.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\rho ≈-0.45$

II. There is a strong negative correlation between $x$ and $y.$

III. There is a weak negative correlation between $x$ and $y.$

Hint: $|\rho |>0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation." :question/worked-solution "The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho |<0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. To calculate $\rho ,$ we first compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(10-15)(3-4)+(15-15)(6-4) \\  & +(12-15)(5-4)+(23-15)(2-4) \\  & =(-5)(-1)+(0)(2)+(-3)(1)+(8)(-2) \\  & =5+0-3-16 \\  & =-14\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(10-15)^{2}+(15-15)^{2}+(12-15)^{2}+(23-15)^{2} \\  & =25+0+9+64 \\  & =98 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(3-4)^{2}+(6-4)^{2}+(5-4)^{2}+(2-4)^{2} \\  & =1+4+1+4 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{-14}{\sqrt{98}\cdot \sqrt{10}} \\  & ≈-\frac{14}{9.899\,495\cdot 3.162\,278} \\  & ≈-0.45,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false while statement III is true. Since $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is weak. Also, since $\rho $ is negative, the correlation is negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b0ac2d8e-1510-54ca-9445-4aec50f70251"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-b0ac2d8e-1510-54ca-9445-4aec50f70251" :answer-field/id #uuid "b0ac2d8e-1510-54ca-9445-4aec50f70251" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ce4b8373-460f-5dbf-8df7-974dfa84cfd5" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ce4b8373-460f-5dbf-8df7-974dfa84cfd5" "answer-3e641f3d-eaf3-5390-a911-b775f5999ebc" "answer-1f0401d4-997c-5e0e-a92c-bddf630c789e" "answer-fb05b1cb-d912-53a1-83e4-41068da91e3c" "answer-0b9b6447-5e81-5ee1-b93e-f349481ecf21"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ce4b8373-460f-5dbf-8df7-974dfa84cfd5" :answer/id #uuid "ce4b8373-460f-5dbf-8df7-974dfa84cfd5" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I and III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3e641f3d-eaf3-5390-a911-b775f5999ebc" :answer/id #uuid "3e641f3d-eaf3-5390-a911-b775f5999ebc" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "I only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1f0401d4-997c-5e0e-a92c-bddf630c789e" :answer/id #uuid "1f0401d4-997c-5e0e-a92c-bddf630c789e" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "II only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-fb05b1cb-d912-53a1-83e4-41068da91e3c" :answer/id #uuid "fb05b1cb-d912-53a1-83e4-41068da91e3c" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "III only" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-0b9b6447-5e81-5ee1-b93e-f349481ecf21" :answer/id #uuid "0b9b6447-5e81-5ee1-b93e-f349481ecf21" :answer/type :answer.type/text :answer/value "None" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5218551b-c171-5334-a3fb-989e7c3fce63" :question/id #uuid "5218551b-c171-5334-a3fb-989e7c3fce63" :question/math-academy-id "q-134359" :question/problem "Olivia plays soccer. "A teacher of a group of $4$ students wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between $x,$ the number of hours the students had slept the night before an exam, and $y,$ the student's score in the exam. The data is shown below. 

| **Number of hours** | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Score ** | $56$ | $68$ | $81$ | $79$ |

You are given that the means are $\overset{―}{x}=5$ and $\overset{―}{y}=71.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\rho ≈0.81$

II. There is a strong positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

III. There is a weak positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

*Hint: $|\rho |>0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation.*" :question/worked-solution "The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho |<0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is false. To calculate $\rho ,$ we first compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(2-5)(56-71)+(4-5)(68-71) \\  & +(6-5)(81-71)+(8-5)(79-71) \\  & =(-3)(-15)+(-1)(-3)+(1)(10)+(3)(8) \\  & =45+3+10+24 \\  & =82\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(2-5)^{2}+(4-5)^{2}+(6-5)^{2}+(8-5)^{2} \\  & =9+1+1+9 \\  & =20 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(56-71)^{2}+(68-71)^{2}+(81-71)^{2}+(79-71)^{2} \\  & =225+9+100+64 \\  & =398\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{82}{\sqrt{20}\cdot \sqrt{398}} \\  & ≈\frac{82}{4.472\,136\cdot 19.949\,937} \\  & ≈0.92,\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Since $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is strong. Also, since $\rho $ is positive, the correlation is positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bf65d2d2-724d-5cf1-bd32-eea27646ffc4"] :db/ensure - if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

$$

It is often denoted by $\rho$ for a population and by $r$ for a sample. In this lesson, we'll concern ourselves with population data only. 

The linear correlation coefficient satisfies the following constraint:

$$
-1 \leq \rho \leq 1
$$

We interpret the endpoints of this interval as follows:

- $\rho = 1$ means that there is a perfect *positive* correlation between the data points.

- $\rho = -1$ means that there is a perfect *negative* correlation between the data points.

Moreover, $\rho = 0$ means there is no *linear* correlation between the data points. 

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- If $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is **strong,** and the data points closely follow a straight line. 

![](images/3f/3fd8b4e85bd76bbf78fdb2b135c49b3fd5e37fd9651dcae29d945d75aa45b905.png)

- If $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,$ the correlation is **weak.** The data points follow a straight line, but many are far from the line.

![](images/c1/c132ec90770bb84ad6c7dcc4b24773a923139c616f523ba0a23c1506c40c508c.png)

- If $|\rho| \lt 0.3,$ then the correlation is **negligible.** There is no (linear) correlation.

![](images/9a/9afa80bfadc40b8b832b17dcea10d66d5a08955909d5bea66c7c010558b5ea19.png)" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097902 :tutorial/content "To calculate $\rho,$ we use the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

- $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance between $x$ and $y,$ and

- $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations of $x$ and $y,$ respectively.

For example, consider data sets $x$ and $y$ such that 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y)=-9, \qquad \sigma_x=6, \qquad \sigma_y=2.
$$

Substituting our numbers into the formula above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-9)}{(6)\cdot (2)} \\  & =\frac{(-9)}{12} \\  & =-0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is strong. Also, since $\rho$ is negative, the correlation is negative.

Therefore, there is a strong negative correlation between $x$ and $y.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ of the same size.

Let's now introduce the following notation:

$$
S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{yy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\overline{y})^2,
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Notice that $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ are the sums of square deviations found in the formulas for the variance of $x,$ the variance of $y,$ and covariance of $x$ and $y,$ respectively. 

Using the previous definition, we can show that the correlation coefficient can be calculated as follows:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}\,.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097903 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the following result:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
$$

We start with the definition of the correlation coefficient $\rho\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

We have

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = \dfrac1n \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}) = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{n}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n}} \\ {\sigma }_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our definition for $\rho,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}{{n}^{2}}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}{n})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\cancel{n}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}{\cancel{n}})} \\  & =\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096858 :activity/expected-seconds 780.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092240 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d27eb9e3-1a36-5293-b88b-ba67a6d55870"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186092722 :question/problem "The equation of the normal line to the curve $y=2{x}^{2}$ at the point $(2,8)$ is given by $x+py=q$ where $p$ and $q$ are constants. Find the value of $p+q.$" :question/worked-solution "Let $f(x)=2{x}^{2}.$ First, we compute the derivative:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2})=4x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the slope of the tangent at the point $(2,8):$

$$
\begin{aligned}m={f}^{′}(2)=4(2)=8\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the normal line ${m}^{′}$ is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{8}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-8 & =-\frac{1}{8}(x-2) \\ 8y-64 & =-x+2 \\ x+8y & =66.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $p+q=8+66=74.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186090532 :answer-field/correct 17592186090534 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "question-d27eb9e3-1a36-5293-b88b-ba67a6d55870" :question/id #uuid "d27eb9e3-1a36-5293-b88b-ba67a6d55870" :question/math-academy-id "q-342187" :question/problem "Find the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=4x-\frac{2}{x}$ at the point $(-1,-2).$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $15\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $14\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{24}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$ Find, in amperes, the amount of current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $2\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](images/e4/e44f91621134e91a9f742811897940b87ffc24bea4b15100e43d2aa15a8c4330.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=14\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=14I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{24}}=24q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
15=14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(15) & =\frac{d}{dt}(14I+24q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =14\,\frac{dI}{dt}+24\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+7\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+12I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-4t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-4t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{15}{2}-7I-12q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{15}{2}-7I(0)-12q(0) \\  & =\frac{15}{2}-7\cdot 2-12\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{19}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-4B{e}^{-4t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{19}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{19}{2} & =-3A{e}^{-0}-4B{e}^{-0} \\ -\frac{19}{2} & =-3A-4B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2=A+B \\ -\frac{19}{2}=-3A-4B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{3}{2}$ and $B=\frac{7}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-4t}.
$$

Finally, the current in the circuit after $0.3$ seconds, in amperes, is

$$
I(0.3)=-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-0.9}+\frac{7}{2}{e}^{-1.2}≈0.444,
$$

rounded to three decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-8c9be830-6e08-534d-b109-3e3cae593612"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id #uuid "8da21d86-c5a3-5a9d-afe5-a4fc0cdf2ebd" :question/math-academy-id "q-345408" :question/problem "![](images/8a/8a4951e6e156fad815b6b21376031b003f61a986a399bed712709272c1ae6409.png)

Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ in the circuit at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}+\frac{P}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{Q}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),
$$

where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=6I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)=6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+2I=-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+2{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+3(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ +2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) \\ (-2\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-6\alpha -2\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2\alpha +6\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -6\alpha -2\beta =-4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{3}{5}$ and $\beta =\frac{1}{5}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}+\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=3$ and $Q=1,$ and

$$
P+Q=3+1=4.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-139a8209-37f8-5a7e-ba36-31b603338e18"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "Solve the equation ${log}_{2}⁡(2x-5)=\frac{1}{3}{log}_{2}⁡(27).$" :question/worked-solution "First, we use the power rule to simplify the right-hand side. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(2x-5) & =\frac{1}{3}{log}_{2}⁡(27) \\ {log}_{2}⁡(2x-5) & ={log}_{2}⁡({27}^{1/3}) \\ {log}_{2}⁡(2x-5) & ={log}_{2}⁡(3).\end{aligned}
$$

Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(2x-5) & ={log}_{2}⁡(3) \\ 2x-5 & =3 \\ 2x & =8 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation: 

- Substituting $x=4$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{2}⁡(2x-5) & ={log}_{2}⁡(2(4)-5) \\  & ={log}_{2}⁡(3) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{log}_{2}⁡(27).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=4$ is a valid solution." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-389631a9-06db-578a-b331-cd015ccdd6d5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} $$

$$

$$

"Solve the equation ${log}_{6}⁡({x}^{2}+20)={log}_{6}⁡(-10x-5).$" :question/worked-solution "Since the logarithms on both sides of the equation have the same base, we can equate the arguments. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{6}⁡({x}^{2}+20) & ={log}_{6}⁡(-10x-5) \\ {x}^{2}+20 & =-10x-5 \\ {x}^{2}+10x+25 & =0 \\ (x+5)^{2} & =0 \\ x & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's now check for extraneous solutions by substituting back into the original equation:

- Substituting $x=-5$ back into the original equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{log}_{6}⁡({x}^{2}+20) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{6}⁡(-10x-5) \\ {log}_{6}⁡((-5)^{2}+20) & \overset{?}{=}{log}_{6}⁡(-10(-5)-5) \\ {log}_{6}⁡(45) & ={log}_{6}⁡(45).\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=-5$ is a valid solution." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-fc88efbc-b8e0-5750-b595-44d875bff8cc"] :db/ensure ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{6{x}^{7}-3{x}^{3}-4}{2{x}^{5}+7}=$

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we divide both the numerator and the denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{5}.$ Then, by noting that the reciprocals shrink to $0$ in the limit, we can then evaluate the resulting expression.

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{6{x}^{7}-3{x}^{3}-4}{2{x}^{5}+7} & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(\frac{6{x}^{7}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{5}}-\frac{4}{{x}^{5}})}{(\frac{2{x}^{5}}{{x}^{5}}+\frac{7}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{(6{x}^{2}-\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{4}{{x}^{3}})}{(2+\frac{7}{{x}^{5}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }\,\,\frac{6{x}^{2}-0-0}{2+0} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -\infty }3{x}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-47f4facf-bcde-5c7b-98da-d06ed85acb33"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "bc404082-c599-5306-899d-26fb5a707805" :question/math-academy-id "q-114875" :question/problem "Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=3{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x=\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(3{x}^{2})(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2})(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x) & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =x(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2})\cdot 1\,dx \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,dx \\  & =-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+D\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-3\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}-3(-\frac{x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-3D.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}3{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{3{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{2}+\frac{3x\operatorname{cos}⁡(2x)}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)}{4}]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3{(\frac{\pi }{2})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )}{2}+\frac{3(\frac{\pi }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )}{4}-(\frac{3(0)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)}{2}+\frac{3(0)\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)}{2}-\frac{3\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)}{4}) \\  & =0+\frac{3\pi (-1)}{4}-0-0 \\  & =-\frac{3\pi }{4}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-60100382-bef0-5d40-8e4e-57031710307e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-60100382-bef0-5d40-8e4e-57031710307e" :answer-field/id #uuid "60100382-bef0-5d40-8e4e-57031710307e" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-ea372be5-00ac-5d06-b324-96a9d214c32b" :answer-field/choices ["answer-ea372be5-00ac-5d06-b324-96a9d214c32b" "answer-a47b0af8-b237-5b70-8f37-b67b00a01cef" "answer-71e229f8-046f-5d88-8cf3-15d0ca09c39a" "answer-6f2ba34b-4251-5e97-822e-7d6f89fec290" "answer-52851b61-8b9c-53cc-91c6-5200fa78f1ed"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ea372be5-00ac-5d06-b324-96a9d214c32b" :answer/id #uuid "ea372be5-00ac-5d06-b324-96a9d214c32b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{3\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-a47b0af8-b237-5b70-8f37-b67b00a01cef" :answer/id #uuid "a47b0af8-b237-5b70-8f37-b67b00a01cef" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-71e229f8-046f-5d88-8cf3-15d0ca09c39a" :answer/id #uuid "71e229f8-046f-5d88-8cf3-15d0ca09c39a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6f2ba34b-4251-5e97-822e-7d6f89fec290" :answer/id #uuid "6f2ba34b-4251-5e97-822e-7d6f89fec290" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3\pi }{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-52851b61-8b9c-53cc-91c6-5200fa78f1ed" :answer/id #uuid "52851b61-8b9c-53cc-91c6-5200fa78f1ed" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{\pi }{4}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-88eae5cb-fb52-512e-a423-9c404ac93779" :question/id #uuid "88eae5cb-fb52-512e-a423-9c404ac93779" :question/math-academy-id "q-346501" :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. Do not round the answer.

${\int }_{1}^{e}18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x=$
{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=18{x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 18{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=6{x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(6{x}^{3})-\int (6{x}^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡x(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-12(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{3}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =6{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}-12D \\  & ={x}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4}{3})+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-12D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}18{x}^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & ={[{x}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{4}{3})]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =[{e}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡e+\frac{4}{3})]-[{1}^{3}(6{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡1+\frac{4}{3})] \\  & =[{e}^{3}(6-4+\frac{4}{3})]-\frac{4}{3} \\  & =\frac{10{e}^{3}-4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e456e79c-9696-5fd5-914c-4b58ab494688"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id approximate $P(X=50).$ Give your final answer to three decimal places

*Hint: The data below is taken from the table of values of the cumulative distribution function $Φ(z)$ for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.06\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,1.9\,$ | $\,0.9738\,$ | $\,0.9744\,$ | $\,0.9750\,$ |
| $\,2.0\,$ | $\,0.9793\,$ | $\,0.9798\,$ | $\,0.9803\,$ |
| $\,2.1\,$ | $\,0.9838\,$ | $\,0.9842\,$ | $\,0.9846\,$ |
| $\,2.2\,$ | $\,0.9875\,$ | $\,0.9878\,$ | $\,0.9881\,$ |
| $\,2.3\,$ | $\,0.9904\,$ | $\,0.9906\,$ | $\,0.9909\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.4.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.4 \\  & =40 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.4) \\  & =60 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.4)=40
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.4)(1-0.4)=24.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(40,24).$

Now, we can approximate the desired probability $P(X=50).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X=50)≈P(49.5\le Y\le 50.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(49.5\le Y\le 50.5) & =P(\frac{49.5-40}{\sqrt{24}}\le Z\le \frac{50.5-40}{\sqrt{24}}) \\  & ≈P(1.94\le Z\le 2.14) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.14)-P(Z<1.94) \\  & =P(Z\le 2.14)-P(Z\le 1.94) \\  & =Φ(2.14)-Φ(1.94) \\  & =0.9838-0.9738 \\  & =0.010\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=50)≈0.010.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.0102.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186114877 :answer-field/correct 17592186114882 :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115315 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-0c7ac018-c572-51bb-a13b-07a9824c7d91"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-0c7ac018-c572-51bb-a13b-07a9824c7d91" :question/id #uuid "0c7ac018-c572-51bb-a13b-07a9824c7d91" :question/math-academy-id "q-95722" :question/problem "Which of the following probabilities could be approximated using the normal approximation of the binomial distribution?

I. The probability that a student correctly solves $4$ questions in a $5$-question math test if the student has a $75%$ probability of correctly answering each question.

II. The probability that $42$ flights out of $120$ arrive early at an airport if the probability of a single flight arriving early is $0.45$ for each flight.

III. The probability of getting $4$ ones on $10$ rolls of a $4$-sided die." :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Let's now examine each situation.

- In situation I, we have $n=5$ and $p=0.75.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =5\cdot 0.75 \\  & =3.75 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, we *cannot* use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation II, we have $n=120$ and $p=0.45.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =120\cdot 0.45 \\  & =54 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =120\cdot (1-0.45) \\  & =66 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

- In situation III, we have $n=10$ and $p=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =10\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =2.5 \\  & ≯5.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, we *cannot* use the normal approximation of the binomial distribution.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-26bcb8a5-120e-5253-aed0-dce7591e9442"] :db/ensure - $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=60$ and $p=0.44.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =60\cdot 0.44 \\  & =26.4 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =60\cdot (1-0.44) \\  & =33.6 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(60)(0.44)=26.4
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(60)(0.44)(1-0.44)=14.784.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(26.4,14.784).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(X>30).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(X>30)=P(X\ge 31)≈P(Y\ge 30.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 30.5) & =P(Z\ge \frac{30.5-26.4}{\sqrt{14.784}}) \\  & ≈P(Z\ge 1.07) \\  & =1-P(Z<1.07) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 1.07) \\  & =1-Φ(1.07) \\  & =1-0.8577 \\  & =0.1423\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X>30)≈0.142.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.1431.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields $$

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =70\cdot 0.5 \\  & =35 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =70\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =35 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\mu =np=(70)(0.5)=35
$$

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(70)(0.5)(1-0.5)=17.5.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(35,17.5).$

$$
P(X=30)≈P(29.5\le Y\le 30.5).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}P(29.5\le Y\le 30.5) & =P(\frac{29.5-35}{\sqrt{17.5}}\le Z\le \frac{30.5-35}{\sqrt{17.5}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.31\le Z\le -1.08) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.08)-P(Z<-1.31) \\  & =P(Z\le -1.08)-P(Z\le -1.31) \\  & =Φ(-1.08)-Φ(-1.31) \\  & =0.1401-0.0951 \\  & =0.045\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(X=30)≈0.045.
$$

</tbody></table>" :question/worked-solution "Given a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ if 

- $np>5,$ and

- $n(1-p)>5,$

we can approximate $X$ as a normal random variable $Y$ with mean $\mu =np$ and variance ${\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p),$ that is, 

$$
Y∼N(np,np(1-p)).
$$

Here, we have $n=100$ and $p=0.5.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}np & =100\cdot 0.5 \\  & =50 \\  & >5\,✓ \\ n(1-p) & =100\cdot (1-0.5) \\  & =50 \\  & >5.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can approximate our binomial random variable $X$ with a normal random variable $Y$ with mean

$$
\mu =np=(100)(0.5)=50
$$

and variance

$$
{\sigma }^{2}=np(1-p)=(100)(0.5)(1-0.5)=25.
$$

That is, we can approximate $X$ by $Y∼N(50,25).$

Now, we can estimate the desired probability $P(43<X<53).$ Using a continuity correction, we have

$$
P(43<X<53)=P(44\le X\le 52)≈P(43.5\le Y\le 52.5).
$$

To compute this probability, we transform to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(43.5\le Y\le 52.5) & =P(\frac{43.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}\le Z\le \frac{52.5-50}{\sqrt{25}}) \\  & ≈P(-1.30\le Z\le 0.50) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.50)-P(Z<-1.30) \\  & =P(Z\le 0.50)-P(Z\le -1.30) \\  & =Φ(0.50)-Φ(-1.30) \\  & =0.6915-0.0968 \\  & =0.5947\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(43<X<53)≈0.595.
$$

Note: Using a software package for the approximation gives a probability of $0.5947.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields :question/id #uuid "f484bd1c-f53f-587d-99ce-e7d9cbfcb8f5" :question/math-academy-id "q-336663" :question/problem "A tank initially holds $450\,\text{gal}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $18\,\text{lb}$ of sugar.
Fresh water is poured into the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed sugar solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
Find an equation for the amount of sugar $Q(t),$ in pounds, in the tank $t$ minutes after the fresh water is first added." :question/worked-solution "Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the tank minus the rate at which sugar leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a solution containing $0\,\text{lb/gal}$ of sugar) enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the tank.

Now, to find the rate at which sugar leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of solution in the tank at time $t.$

- The tank initially contains $450\,\text{gal}$ of solution.

- Fresh water enters the tank at a rate of $15\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $15t\,\text{gal}$ have entered the tank.

- The completely mixed solution leaves the tank at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, after $t$ minutes, $10t\,\text{gal}$ have left the tank.

As a result, the volume of solution in the tank after $t$ minutes is 

$$
450+15t-10t=(450+5t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Then, since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the tank, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{450+5t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{90+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =0-\frac{2Q}{90+t} \\ \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t}\,Q.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{90+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{90+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{90+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-2\operatorname{ln}⁡|90+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(90+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ \frac{A}{(90+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ A & =18\cdot {90}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=18{(\frac{90}{90+t})}^{2}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-3f739ba7-4312-53fa-a7d7-8241e430155b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id initially holds $500\,\text{L}$ of a sugar-water solution containing $15\,\text{kg}$ of dissolved sugar.
Pure water is pumped into the vat at a rate of $14\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves the vat at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min}.$
Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water pumping begins." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of sugar in the vat at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which sugar enters the vat minus the rate at which sugar leaves the vat.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which sugar enters the vat.

Note that pure water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of sugar) enters the vat at a rate of $14\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *sugar* enters the vat is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}})\cdot (14\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which sugar exits the vat.

To find the rate at which sugar leaves the vat, we first determine the volume of solution in the vat at time $t.$

The vat initially contains $500\,\text{L}$ of solution; water enters at $14\,\text{L/min}$ and drains out at $10\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the vat after $t$ minutes is 

$$
500+14t-10t=(500+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of sugar in the vat, the *concentration* of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed sugar-water solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{L/min},$ *sugar* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{L}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\cancel{\text{L}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{500+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{2(125+t)}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{2(125+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{2(125+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{5}{2(125+t)})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-\frac{5}{2}\int \frac{1}{125+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{-\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡|125+t|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(125+t)^{5/2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the vat initially contains $15\,\text{kg}$ of sugar. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=15,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =15 \\ \frac{A}{(125+0)^{5/2}} & =15 \\ A & =15\cdot {125}^{5/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
Q(t)=15{(\frac{125}{125+t})}^{5/2}
$$

Finally, the amount of sugar in the vat $14$ minutes after the water is first pumped in is

$$
Q(12)=15{(\frac{125}{139})}^{5/2}≈11.50\,\text{kg},
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-32b609db-0cfa-50ce-be77-ccca954943ac"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-32b609db-0cfa-50ce-be77-ccca954943ac" :answer-field/id #uuid "32b609db-0cfa-50ce-be77-ccca954943ac" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-2d0131b4-d374-5e74-aa90-c8abda4a45ee" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6a8e3067-e0d5-573d-b2a5-05f7346c88a9" "answer-2d0131b4-d374-5e74-aa90-c8abda4a45ee" "answer-3001be2d-0b44-511f-939d-52802b97e714" "answer-74737ad0-325a-5620-b4cf-42637b26fb86" "answer-8a1829c7-cd54-5a8c-b939-0c1b1390639f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6a8e3067-e0d5-573d-b2a5-05f7346c88a9" :answer/id #uuid "6a8e3067-e0d5-573d-b2a5-05f7346c88a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "10.84\,\text{kg}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-2d0131b4-d374-5e74-aa90-c8abda4a45ee" :answer/id #uuid "2d0131b4-d374-5e74-aa90-c8abda4a45ee" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "11.50\,\text{kg}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3001be2d-0b44-511f-939d-52802b97e714" :answer/id #uuid "3001be2d-0b44-511f-939d-52802b97e714" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "11.96\,\text{kg}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-74737ad0-325a-5620-b4cf-42637b26fb86" :answer/id #uuid "74737ad0-325a-5620-b4cf-42637b26fb86" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12.31\,\text{kg}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8a1829c7-cd54-5a8c-b939-0c1b1390639f" :answer/id #uuid "8a1829c7-cd54-5a8c-b939-0c1b1390639f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "12.98\,\text{kg}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186115796 :question/problem "A $9\,800\,\text{mL}$-capacity tank initially holds $7\,000\,\text{mL}$ of a brine (salt-water) solution containing $196\,\text{g}$ of salt. Fresh water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $105\,\text{mL/s},$ while the completely mixed brine flows out at a rate of $70\,\text{mL/s}.$ Find the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of salt in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in seconds. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the tank minus the rate at which salt leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{g}/\text{s}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the tank.

First, note that fresh water (i.e., a brine solution containing $0\,\text{g/mL}$ of salt) enters the tank at a rate of $105\,\text{mL/s}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the tank is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}})\cdot (105\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =(0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}})\cdot (105\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the tank.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of brine in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $7\,000\,\text{mL}$ of brine; fresh water enters at $105\,\text{mL/s},$ and mixed brine leaves at $70\,\text{mL/s}.$
As a result, the amount of brine in the tank after $t$ seconds is 

$$
V(t)=7\,000+105t-70t=35(200+t)\,\text{mL}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the tank, the concentration of the brine at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{35(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed brine leaves at a rate of $70\,\text{mL/s},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(70\,\frac{\text{mL}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{35(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{mL}}) \\  & =(70\,\frac{\cancel{\text{mL}}}{\text{s}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{35(200+t)}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\cancel{\text{mL}}}) \\  & =\frac{2Q}{200+t}\,\frac{\text{g}}{\text{s}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{2Q}{200+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{2}{200+t}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{2}{200+t} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt}dt & =\int (-\frac{2}{200+t})\,dt \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\cdot \,dQ & =-2\int \frac{1}{200+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|200+t|)+C \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-2}|+C \\ |Q| & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|(200+t)^{-2}|+C} \\ Q(t) & =\frac{A}{(200+t)^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $A=\pm {e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration.

We're told that the tank initially contains $196\,\text{g}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=196,$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =196 \\ \frac{A}{(200+0)^{2}} & =196 \\ A & =196(200)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =\frac{196(200)^{2}}{(200+t)^{2}} \\  & =196{(\frac{200}{200+t})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $9\,800\,\text{mL},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=9\,800$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =9\,800 \\ 35(200+{t}_{o}) & =9\,800 \\ 200+{t}_{o} & =280 \\ {t}_{o} & =80\,\text{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of salt in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(80) & =196{(\frac{200}{200+80})}^{2} \\  & =196{(\frac{5}{7})}^{2} \\  & =100\,\text{g}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186113713 :answer-field/correct "answer-6eccbf39-7b81-5f1c-9b9b-de95bddd15ef" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6eccbf39-7b81-5f1c-9b9b-de95bddd15ef" "answer-1625cbd3-6d04-52bf-ad57-d5116e771c6a" "answer-81039cc6-be6e-5a3d-9d5d-380bf1e7265b" "answer-ce095df2-3455-538e-9ce0-230be6f286f5" "answer-86f58fcb-92e0-5aca-9ded-ec1b4b86eec8"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6eccbf39-7b81-5f1c-9b9b-de95bddd15ef" :answer/id #uuid "6eccbf39-7b81-5f1c-9b9b-de95bddd15ef" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "100\,\text{g}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-1625cbd3-6d04-52bf-ad57-d5116e771c6a" :answer/id #uuid "1625cbd3-6d04-52bf-ad57-d5116e771c6a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "102\,\text{g}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-81039cc6-be6e-5a3d-9d5d-380bf1e7265b" :answer/id #uuid "81039cc6-be6e-5a3d-9d5d-380bf1e7265b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "105\,\text{g}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ce095df2-3455-538e-9ce0-230be6f286f5" :answer/id #uuid "ce095df2-3455-538e-9ce0-230be6f286f5" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "110\,\text{g}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86f58fcb-92e0-5aca-9ded-ec1b4b86eec8" :answer/id #uuid "86f58fcb-92e0-5aca-9ded-ec1b4b86eec8" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "120\,\text{g}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-3404cdf4-fad8-57cc-99a9-cffaef1b2f88" :question/id #uuid "3404cdf4-fad8-57cc-99a9-cffaef1b2f88" :question/math-academy-id "q-336839" :question/problem "A $500\,\text{L}$-capacity water tank initially holds $320\,\text{L}$ of water containing $20\,\text{kg}$ of a dissolved contaminant. Clean water begins to flow into the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{L/min},$ while the completely mixed water flows out at a rate of $5\,\text{L/min}.$ Find, rounded to two decimal places, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow." :question/worked-solution "Let $Q$ be the amount of contaminant in the tank at time $t.$ Then, the derivative

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which contaminant enters the tank minus the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{kg/min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant enters the tank.

First, note that clean water (i.e., water containing $0\,\text{kg/L}$ of contaminant) enters the tank at a rate of $9\,\text{L/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *contaminant* enters the tank is

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}})\cdot (9\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =0\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which contaminant exits the tank.

To find the rate at which contaminant leaves the tank, we must first determine the volume of water in the tank at time $t.$

The tank initially contains $320\,\text{L}$ of water; clean water enters at $9\,\text{L/min},$ and mixed water leaves at $5\,\text{L/min}.$
As a result, the amount of water in the tank after $t$ minutes is

$$
V(t)=320+9t-5t=(320+4t)\,\text{L}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the tank is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of contaminant in the tank, the *concentration* of the water at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed water leaves at a rate of $5\,\text{L/min},$ *contaminant* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(5\,\frac{\text{L}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{L}}) \\  & =\frac{5Q}{320+4t}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{5Q}{4(80+t)}\,\frac{\text{kg}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =0-\frac{5Q}{4(80+t)},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}=-\frac{5}{4(80+t)}\,Q.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

Separating variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}\cdot \frac{dQ}{dt} & =-\frac{5}{4(80+t)} \\ \int \frac{1}{Q}\,dQ & =-\frac{5}{4}\int \frac{1}{80+t}\,dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|Q| & =-\frac{5}{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡|80+t|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus,

$$
Q(t)=\frac{A}{(80+t)^{5/4}}.
$$

Using the initial condition $Q(0)=20,$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{A}{{80}^{5/4}} & =20 \\ A & =20(80)^{5/4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So,

$$
Q(t)=20{(\frac{80}{80+t})}^{5/4}.
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. Since the tank has a capacity of $500\,\text{L},$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =500 \\ 320+4{t}_{o} & =500 \\ 4{t}_{o} & =180 \\ {t}_{o} & =45\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the amount of contaminant in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(45)7 & =20{(\frac{80}{80+45})}^{5/4} \\  & =20{(\frac{80}{125})}^{5/4} \\  & ≈11.45\,\text{kg},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a2296ad1-b5ad-5318-8ca2-47375c1f24ea"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186198944 :question/problem "![](images/72/720713e7e1dbfbc9ce3ebb486e8744327c633745d00df7dc862d794eefe57bbc.png)

What is the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ and the point $(4,0)?$" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-7x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-7 & =0 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-7(\frac{7}{2})+16} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0,$ so $x=1$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+5} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-a9413410-1a9d-50b7-9182-e546f0368ec5"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-a9413410-1a9d-50b7-9182-e546f0368ec5" :answer-field/id #uuid "a9413410-1a9d-50b7-9182-e546f0368ec5" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-d2c19332-1daa-53e4-8c7e-f6edf5736887" :answer-field/choices ["answer-d2c19332-1daa-53e4-8c7e-f6edf5736887"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d2c19332-1daa-53e4-8c7e-f6edf5736887" :answer/id #uuid "d2c19332-1daa-53e4-8c7e-f6edf5736887" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\sqrt{3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-ceab1153-db5f-5530-aee8-9a4937774de9" :question/id #uuid "ceab1153-db5f-5530-aee8-9a4937774de9" :question/math-academy-id "q-344849" :question/problem "Find the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2$ and the point $P(2,2).$ Do not round the answer.

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{|x-1|}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-ae0782a8-a8ce-5695-a710-1fed57c8a4e2"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id Given that $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 18,$ find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{25}=5, \\ \text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[Y]}=\sqrt{36}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[X]} \\  & =\frac{18}{5\cdot 6} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162141 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-7da918be-db4c-59cf-8e95-bb2e34ce04e6" "question-77a83823-b66d-5cc9-b223-222b52ef5845"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161707 :question/problem "| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $f_X$ |

| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ | $0.4$ |
| $f_Y$ | $0.4$ | $0.6$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\textrm {E}[X]=0.4\qquad
\textrm {E}[Y]=0.6, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X] \approx 0.4899, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y] \approx 0.4899,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.5 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.1-(0.4)(0.6) \\  & =-0.14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.14}{0.4899\cdot 0.4899} \\  & ≈-0.58,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186162142 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-db6e411e-8a97-527f-83cb-17311240c8a4" "question-2265fb13-ede5-5876-96c9-a4518515ab31" "question-37a89027-b700-5936-918f-1cda621eae37" "question-6da1a8e2-af30-5f0e-8a87-d537d126dcee" "question-86de9def-10fe-5788-a466-3607900726ce"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186161708 :question/problem "![](images/9c/9cf18d64c3f283c730e1d32ee81e3f193e615bb7b0b936dac009c46328826b3d.svg)

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xy\cdot 2(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}(2{x}^{2}y+2x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{5}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{x+y}{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-(\frac{11}{9})(\frac{5}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{81}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(-\frac{1}{81})}{(0.5329)\cdot (0.2833)} \\  & ≈-0.08,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-abcaf86c-3cea-5f12-a174-9ce2866296f7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-abcaf86c-3cea-5f12-a174-9ce2866296f7" :answer-field/id #uuid "abcaf86c-3cea-5f12-a174-9ce2866296f7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-b56517bb-ec5e-584d-9307-e3e474bb3360" :answer-field/choices ["answer-64e5f106-8480-5a83-97f5-e5174d418982" "answer-b56517bb-ec5e-584d-9307-e3e474bb3360" "answer-304f73f4-0397-5854-960b-762988f4153d" "answer-62ec7766-2c11-5907-b71d-e497ceab6d8f" "answer-dcb85af9-dc03-5f44-8022-ff6dccdd0429"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-64e5f106-8480-5a83-97f5-e5174d418982" :answer/id #uuid "64e5f106-8480-5a83-97f5-e5174d418982" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-0.04" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-b56517bb-ec5e-584d-9307-e3e474bb3360" :answer/id #uuid "b56517bb-ec5e-584d-9307-e3e474bb3360" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-0.08" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-304f73f4-0397-5854-960b-762988f4153d" :answer/id #uuid "304f73f4-0397-5854-960b-762988f4153d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-0.12" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-62ec7766-2c11-5907-b71d-e497ceab6d8f" :answer/id #uuid "62ec7766-2c11-5907-b71d-e497ceab6d8f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.06" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-dcb85af9-dc03-5f44-8022-ff6dccdd0429" :answer/id #uuid "dcb85af9-dc03-5f44-8022-ff6dccdd0429" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "0.15" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-37a89027-b700-5936-918f-1cda621eae37" :question/id #uuid "37a89027-b700-5936-918f-1cda621eae37" :question/math-academy-id "q-148419" :question/problem "$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot (\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{2{y}^{2}}{x}+\frac{1}{2}xy)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{3x}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{2}{3x}+\frac{1}{4}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}+\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}+\frac{3}{8})-(\frac{3}{4}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)(\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}-\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12})+(\frac{3}{8}-\frac{7}{16}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12}-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)]_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(-y)]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)\frac{\pi }{2}+1-(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}.\end{aligned}

$$
