:question/problem "Evaluate the integral $\displaystyle \int_0^1 (t^2+1)e^{2t+1} \, \textrm{d} t.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={t}^{2}+1\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2}+1)(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int t\,e^{2t+1}\,\textrm{d}t.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t=\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t)(\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{2})(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\int t\,{e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-(\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}}{2}-\frac{t\,{e}^{2t+1}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}-D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}(2{t}^{2}-2t+3)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -{D}.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+1){e}^{2t+1}\,\text{d}t & ={[\frac{{e}^{2t+1}}{4}(2{t}^{2}-2t+3)]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{{e}^{2(1)+1}}{4}(2(1)^{2}-2(1)+3))-(\frac{{e}^{2(0)+1}}{4}(2(0)^{2}-2(0)+3)) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3}}{4}(2-2+3)-\frac{e}{4}(0-0+3) \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{3}}{4}-\frac{3e}{4} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{3}-3e}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186050929} {:db/id 17592186069032 :question/id #uuid "5a014a29-8bc7-5ab9-a7b1-a2c515a94e18" :question/math-academy-id "q-12700"} {:db/id 17592186069034 :question/id #uuid "5d1eaea1-7b15-5705-a2f1-f87963943a22" :question/math-academy-id "q-12707"} {:db/id 17592186250302 :question/id #uuid "1074dd87-580f-51cd-9b83-51cf6a648213" :question/math-academy-id "q-114693"} {:db/id 17592186250303 :question/id #uuid "c11ce04f-84d3-5cfd-9c93-5cd848d912ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-114695"} {:db/id 17592186250306 :question/id #uuid "c03c84f2-a54b-5cd7-81f9-a3bec98efab8" :question/math-academy-id "q-114699"} {:db/id 17592186262689 :question/id #uuid "e9224047-f3da-5bf1-a76d-027468545ef6" :question/math-academy-id "q-12703"} {:db/id 17592186320931 :question/id #uuid "584ef325-c160-50e3-98bc-6bcc9919543d" :question/math-academy-id "q-351977"} {:db/id 17592186320933 :question/id #uuid "1a2f1472-983a-5988-9015-40ac8b729fa5" :question/math-academy-id "q-351983" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186068919 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b69f026a-50b3-505d-bd9d-8b295691b66e" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "6b075ced-5a58-52b1-9238-36dc27c2ec56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3{e}^{4}-3{e}^{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186319719}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "6b075ced-5a58-52b1-9238-36dc27c2ec56" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{3{e}^{4}-3{e}^{2}}{4}" :db/id 17592186319719} :answer-field/id #uuid "0d64743d-9a58-56a2-86a7-e957db42f825" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320187}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={t}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=2t, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3{e}^{2t+2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int 3{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t=\frac{3}{2}{e}^{2t+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =({t}^{2})(\frac{3}{2}{e}^{2t+2})-\int (\frac{3}{2}{e}^{2t+2})(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}-3\int t{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int t{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=1, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}={e}^{2t+2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t=\int {e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t+2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t)(\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t+2})-\int (\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t+2})(1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{2t+2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{2t+2}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2t+2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}-3\int t{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}-3(\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{2t+2}-\frac{1}{4}{e}^{2t+2}+D) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}-\frac{3}{2}t{e}^{2t+2}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t+2}+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-3D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}3{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}\,\text{d}t & =(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{2}{e}^{2t+2}-\frac{3}{2}t{e}^{2t+2}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t+2})\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{3}{2}({1}^{2}){e}^{2(1)+2}-\frac{3}{2}(1){e}^{2(1)+2}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2(1)+2})-(\frac{3}{2}({0}^{2}){e}^{2(0)+2}-\frac{3}{2}(0){e}^{2(0)+2}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2(0)+2}) \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{e}^{4}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2} \\  & =\frac{3{e}^{4}-3{e}^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186320934 :question/id #uuid "e235b03c-6338-5aac-b78a-cee6da78b778" :question/math-academy-id "q-351991" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186068919 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b69f026a-50b3-505d-bd9d-8b295691b66e" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "823c5e0e-13c8-50c5-9177-f0541f81db79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{11{e}^{3}-7e}{4}" :db/id 17592186319786}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "823c5e0e-13c8-50c5-9177-f0541f81db79" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{11{e}^{3}-7e}{4}" :db/id 17592186319786} :answer-field/id #uuid "f0269145-0ae9-55e4-a07c-12dcf8ceee64" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320668}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={y}^{2}+3\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=2y, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}+3){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =({y}^{2}+3)(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}+3){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=y\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}={e}^{2y-1}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y=\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y=\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =(y)(\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})-\int (\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{2})(1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({y}^{2}+3){e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y & =\frac{({y}^{2}+3){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\int y\,{e}^{2y-1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}+3){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-(\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}+D) \\  & =\frac{({y}^{2}+3){e}^{2y-1}}{2}-\frac{y\,{e}^{2y-1}}{2}+\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}-D \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2y-1}}{4}(2{y}^{2}-2y+7)+C,\end{aligned}

where $C=-D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$

:question/worked-solution "In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x) & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2})(\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))-\int (\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{2}{3}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\displaystyle \int x\sin(3x) \textrm{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x) & \,⟹\,v=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x=-\,\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =x(-\,\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))-\int (-\,\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{3}\,x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{3}\,x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{3}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x))+{C}_{1} \\  & =-\,\frac{1}{3}\,x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{9}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{C}_{1}\,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1$ is a constant of integration.
So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{2}{3}\int x\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{2}{3}(-\,\frac{1}{3}\,x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+\frac{1}{9}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+{C}_{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+\frac{2}{9}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{2}{27}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{2{C}_{1}}{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{27}((9{x}^{2}-2)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)+6x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x))+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -\dfrac{2C_1}{3}.$"} {:db/id 17592186050489} {:db/id 17592186069065 :question/id #uuid "2a7ca4f4-8f18-5ed5-ad93-5c4531d898de" :question/math-academy-id "q-14736"} {:db/id 17592186069399 :question/id #uuid "7db8d1cc-8a1b-5f0d-8178-c39bb5e755e0" :question/math-academy-id "q-49931"} {:db/id 17592186319108 :question/id #uuid "0a15a17d-ca7d-59f1-8794-23e0f15ee7e4" :question/math-academy-id "q-346495"} {:db/id 17592186320938 :question/id #uuid "4ab61fbf-dc3d-51ac-b56f-b2bcd435ac6a" :question/math-academy-id "q-352000"} {:db/id 17592186320939 :question/id #uuid "2262c5cf-5d28-5084-b420-d0952eb71a4f" :question/math-academy-id "q-352007"} {:db/id 17592186320940 :question/id #uuid "dd434389-5ff0-5c53-84ec-ba4d8f0f505a" :question/math-academy-id "q-352011"} {:db/id 17592186320941 :question/id #uuid "04a3accc-0ede-53f3-a2b9-91a9f4b47156" :question/math-academy-id "q-352026"} {:db/id 17592186320942 :question/id #uuid "ce8ce801-4acf-5ae8-b6e4-25107fda723b" :question/math-academy-id "q-352028" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186068920 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "d2a41ede-381e-55f6-99e5-1baf1ea348a1" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c8d98ca1-5383-519e-939b-8606ea79f890" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}-4" :db/id 17592186320004}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "c8d98ca1-5383-519e-939b-8606ea79f890" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "{\pi }^{2}-4" :db/id 17592186320004} :answer-field/id #uuid "ded71c5d-94de-520f-9363-1d054bf11cec" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320624}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

$$
\begin{aligned}u=27{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=54x \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x=-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(27{x}^{2})(-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})-\int (-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)}{3})(54x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-9{x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)+18\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=32{x}^{3} & \,⟹\,v=\int 32{x}^{3}\text{d}x=8{x}^{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 32{x}^{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}(8{x}^{4})-\int (8{x}^{4})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-16\int {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\displaystyle\int {x^3\ln(x)} \textrm{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3} & \,⟹\,v=\int {x}^{3}\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)(\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})-\int (\frac{{x}^{4}}{4})(\frac{1}{x})\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{4}-\frac{1}{4}\int {x}^{3}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{4}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{16}+{C}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1$ is an integral constant. So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 32{x}^{3}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)^{2}\text{d}x & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-16\int {x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x \\  & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-16(\frac{{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)}{4}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{16}+{C}_{1}) \\  & =8{x}^{4}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4{x}^{4}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+{x}^{4}-16{C}_{1} \\  & ={x}^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)+C\,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -4C_1.$ Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}32{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)\text{d}x & ={{x}^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(x)+1)|}_{1}^{e} \\  & =[(e)^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(e))}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(e)+1)]-[(1)^{4}(8{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1))}^{2}-4\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)+1)] \\  & =[{e}^{4}(8-4+1)]-1 \\  & =5{e}^{4}-1.\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3}))(x)-\int (x)(\frac{3}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3\int \text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & =x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})-3x+D) \\  & =x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})+18x+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-6D.$ 

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})\,\text{d}x & ={[x{ln}^{2}⁡({x}^{3})-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})+18x]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =[e{ln}^{2}⁡({e}^{3})-6e\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{3})+18e]-[(1){ln}^{2}⁡({1}^{3})-6(1)\operatorname{ln}⁡({1}^{3})+18(1)] \\  & =9e-18e+18e-18 \\  & =9e-18.\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186250319 :question/id #uuid "dca36867-5a6f-51bd-9e64-ad043dde12a1" :question/math-academy-id "q-114900" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186068921 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "98a67346-c2c9-5d22-8adf-479fea81eaa2" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "082f5ffa-db8f-5b86-9f1f-66bec8888277" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2{e}^{2}-1" :db/id 17592186247495} {:answer/id #uuid "312a7284-86a2-58d1-925a-aae469b9cc31" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}+2}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186247869} {:answer/id #uuid "4646f294-569b-5c9a-8e3f-8b4bffc32dd4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{1-2e}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186248052} {:answer/id #uuid "8a1ab61f-f876-54ff-ac9a-719572398e93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186248654} {:answer/id #uuid "aed8ce21-2fef-51ea-932a-bf3d76234eac" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "8e" :db/id 17592186248988}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "8a1ab61f-f876-54ff-ac9a-719572398e93" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}" :db/id 17592186248654} :answer-field/id #uuid "90297971-15bc-5633-a065-ce4100255f03" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186249928}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to use integration by parts. $$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}(2{x}^{2})-\int (2{x}^{2})(\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2-2+1)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(0-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}.\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=3 & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 3\,\text{d}x=3x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}(3x)-\int (3x)(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =3x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}-\int 6\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int 6\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=6 & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 6\,\text{d}x=6x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 6\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)(6x)-\int (6x)(\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-\int 6\,\text{d}x \\  & =6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-6x+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =3x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}-\int 6\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =3x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}-(6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)-6x+D) \\  & =3x(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}-6x\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)+6x-D \\  & =3x((\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1/3}^{e/3}3(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[3x((\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x))^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3x)+2)]}_{1/3}^{e/3} \\  & =[3(\frac{e}{3})({(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot \frac{e}{3}))}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot \frac{e}{3})+2)]-[3(\frac{1}{3})({(\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot \frac{1}{3}))}^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡(3\cdot \frac{1}{3})+2)] \\  & =[e((\operatorname{ln}⁡e)^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)]-[1((\operatorname{ln}⁡1)^{2}-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2)] \\  & =[e(1-2+2)]-[1(0-0+2)] \\  & =e-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186320946 :question/id #uuid "63f87158-db44-5db5-9c59-fd71fce3385d" :question/math-academy-id "q-352049"} {:db/id 17592186320947 :question/id #uuid "4d3bd2be-c388-5990-aa44-fdfa96c596f9" :question/math-academy-id "q-352056" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186068921 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "98a67346-c2c9-5d22-8adf-479fea81eaa2" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "14560af1-da74-5f36-a18b-b748d25b48a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5{e}^{3}-2" :db/id 17592186319448}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "14560af1-da74-5f36-a18b-b748d25b48a9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "5{e}^{3}-2" :db/id 17592186319448} :answer-field/id #uuid "b77a2913-0af3-5bc9-8b65-91a3fcf636d6" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045492 :db/ident :answer-field.type/blank} :db/id 17592186320531}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "Evaluate the following integral. {{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{x+1}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=27(x+1)^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 27(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x=9(x+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27(x+1)^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}(9(x+1)^{3})-\int (9(x+1)^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-18\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x+1}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=(x+1)^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int (x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)(\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int (x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{3}-\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27(x+1)^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-18\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-18(\frac{(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{3}-\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-6(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2(x+1)^{3}-18D \\  & =(x+1)^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-18D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{e-1}27(x+1)^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[(x+1)^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2)]}_{0}^{e-1} \\  & =[{e}^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)]-[{1}^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2)] \\  & =[{e}^{3}(9-6+2)]-2 \\  & =5{e}^{3}-2\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186320956 :question/id #uuid "ebbb3ae8-e373-5e9a-af80-1375d64670c5" :question/math-academy-id "q-352122"} {:db/id 17592186320957 :question/id #uuid $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Now, suppose that we want to calculate $\displaystyle \int x^2e^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ Can we use integration by parts in this case?

Let's  try. We define $u$ and $v$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

So the formula for integration by parts leads to

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & ={x}^{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral  $\displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.$ To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={e}^{4x} & \,⟹\,v=\int {e}^{4x}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x \\  & =x(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})-\int (\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})\cdot 1\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{4}(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{4x})+{C}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}\,,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C_1$ is a constant of integration.
So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}{e}^{4x}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}\int x{e}^{4x}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{2}(\frac{1}{4}\,x{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{4x}+{C}_{1}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\,{x}^{2}{e}^{4x}-\frac{1}{8}\,x{e}^{4x}+\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}-\frac{{C}_{1}}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{32}\,{e}^{4x}(8{x}^{2}-4x+1)+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C = -\dfrac{C_1}{2}.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35a2eb7b-569b-5939-bcc0-2261596617e8" :tutorial/math-academy-id 901 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid For example, consider the linear function $f(x) = 2x,$ graphed below.

![](images/09/09716693ba950bd3d14d0ea008dbd9d99dc51a26f30e87ccbf1559f34329fed9.png)

The graph covers all $y$-values, so the range of the function is

$$
-\infty < y< \infty,
$$

which we can also write as

$$
-\infty < f(x) < \infty.
$$

Furthermore, we can express the range as $f(x)\in (-\infty,\infty)$ using interval notation.

If we restrict the domain, the range also changes. Let's now consider the function

$$
g(x) = 2x, \quad x \in [0,2).
$$

The graph $y = g(x)$ is shown below.

![](images/79/791aca2b232c0eee5950c4c1c87073b4c51cd5d61d094de893ca4a2ec28e8d1e.png)

The $y$ values go from $y=0$ up to (but not including) $y=4,$ including every value in between. Therefore, the range of the function is 

$$
0\leq g(x) < 4.
$$

Using interval notation, we can also write the range as $g(x)\in [0,4).$" :tutorial/id #uuid "35906cd0-d08e-5f2a-b88e-9e8ac1329502" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8801 :tutorial/title "Graphs of Functions"} :step/id #uuid "0e0d7002-1126-53ab-8ffd-a09dbe4a234a" :step/math-academy-id 150957 :step/next {:db/id 17592186084044}} {:db/id 17592186084044 :step/content {:db/id 17592186083180 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186082941 :question/id #uuid "6b1dabe1-f820-5ab8-aceb-bbd5be3029a2" :question/math-academy-id "e-14172"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "f4d624bf-dfd2-5910-a5a6-c72352e76e40" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186083526} {:db/id 17592186083937} {:db/id 17592186488182} {:db/id 17592186488278} {:db/id 17592186489217} {:db/id 17592186489284} {:db/id 17592186490280} {:db/id 17592186490288} {:db/id 17592186507490}] :knowledge-point/title "Identifying a Function's Range From a Graph"} :step/id #uuid "5bd906c2-2b91-5274-869f-0425ba950919" :step/math-academy-id 150958}] :activity/title "The Range of a Function" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186083444} {:db/id 17592186084040 :step/content {:db/id 17592186084518 :tutorial/content "The **range** of a function is the collection of numbers (or set) containing all the function's outputs.

Context"}] :question/problem "A stall selling lemonade is set up at a special four-day summer festival. The stall owner wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between $x$, the temperature at $12\,\textrm{p.m}$, and $y$, the number of cups of lemonade sold that day. The data is shown below.

| **Temperature at<br>$12$ p.m. ($^\circ \mathrm{C}$)** | **$26$** | **$30$** | **$22$** | **$18$** |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| **Cups of Lemonade Sold** | $100$ | $118$ | $124$ | $86$ |

You are given that the means are $\overline{x}=24$ and $\overline{y}=107$. Which of the following statements are true?

1. $\rho\approx 0.54$
2. There is a strong positive correlation between $x$ and $y$.
3. There is a weak positive correlation between $x$ and $y$.

*Hint: $\mid \rho \mid > 0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3 \leq \mid \rho \mid \leq 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation.*" :question/worked-solution "The linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the data sets

$$
x=\big\{x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}
$$

and

$$
y=\big\{y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}
$$

is given by

$$
\rho(x,y) = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $\mid \rho \mid \gt 0.7$, the correlation is *strong*
- if $0.3\leq \mid \rho \mid \leq 0.7$, the correlation is *weak*
- if $\mid \rho \mid \lt 0.3$, then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. To calculate $\rho$, we first compute the sum in the numerator:
$S_{xy}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)); = (26 - 24)(100 - 107) + (30 - 24)(118 - 107); = + (22 - 24)(124 - 107) + (18 - 24)(86 - 107); = (2)(-7) + (6)(11) + (-2)(17) + (-6)(-21); =-14 + 66 - 34 + 126; = 144$
Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:
$S_{xx}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2}; = (26 - 24)^{2} + (30 - 24)^{2} + (22 - 24)^{2} + (18 - 24)^{2}; = 4 + 36 + 4 + 36; = 80; S_{yy}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(y_{i} - y^(―))^{2}; = (100 - 107)^{2} + (118 - 107)^{2} + (124 - 107)^{2} + (86 - 107)^{2}; = 49 + 121 + 289 + 441; = 900$
Finally, we use the formula:
$ρ(x, y)|= \frac{144}{\sqrt{80} \cdot \sqrt{900}}; \approx \frac{144}{8.944272 \cdot 30}; \approx 0.54$,
rounded to $2$ decimal places.
- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $0.3\leq \mid \rho \mid \leq 0.7$ the correlation is weak. Also, since $\rho$ is positive, the correlation is positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only.""} {:db/id 17592186096940 :question/id #uuid "0c8e6cdd-2075-560a-ad21-7e80496b36eb" :question/math-academy-id "q-10847"} {:db/id 17592186097075 :question/id #uuid "ecf23364-706a-507a-acc9-36bc48ac45fb" :question/math-academy-id "q-134191"} {:db/id 17592186096727 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096522 :question/id #uuid "5002af3e-d0f0-59eb-a52d-bfd7d101115e" :question/math-academy-id "e-5725"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "76569338-1e2a-5b12-96ef-685d272343cd" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048914} {:db/id 17592186049126} {:db/id 17592186049976}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096927 :question/id #uuid "2811c370-5b30-5984-8372-c002bcffbf44" :question/math-academy-id "q-10271"} {:db/id 17592186097073 :question/id #uuid "995413dd-72d3-5a38-a3be-4cdee05f1492" :question/math-academy-id "q-134084"}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Correlation Coefficient Using Covariance and Standard Deviations"} {:db/id 17592186096522 :question/id #uuid "5002af3e-d0f0-59eb-a52d-bfd7d101115e" :question/math-academy-id "e-5725" :knowledge-point/_canonical-example [{:db/id 17592186096727 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "76569338-1e2a-5b12-96ef-685d272343cd" :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Correlation Coefficient Using Covariance and Standard Deviations"}] :question/problem "Consider the following data sets:
$x = \big\{6, \: 3, \: -1, \: 0 \big\},\qquad y = \big\{5, \: 7, \: -2, \: 6 \big\}$
You're given that $\overline{x}=2$, $\overline{y}=4$, $\sigma_x \approx 2.739$, and $\sigma_y \approx 3.536$. Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets

$$
x=\big\{x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}
$$

and

$$
y=\big\{y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}
$$

is given by

$$
\rho(x,y) = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y}
$$

where $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Cov(x, y) &= \frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)) \\
&= \frac{1}{4}[(6 - 2)(5 - 4) + (3 - 2)(7 - 4) + (-1 - 2)(-2 - 4) + (0 - 2)(6 - 4)] \\
&= \frac{1}{4}[(4)(1) + (1)(3) + (-3)(-6) + (-2)(2)] \\
&= \frac{1}{4}[4 + 3 + 18 - 4] \\
&= \frac{1}{4} \cdot 21 \\
&= 5.25
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
ρ(x, y) &= (Cov(x, y))/(σ_{x} \cdot σ_{y}) \\
&\approx \frac{5.25}{2.739 \cdot 3.536} \\
&\approx 0.54
\end{aligned}

$x = \big\{13, \: 10, \: 9, \: 12 \big\},\qquad y = \big\{-1, \: 3, \: 2, \: 4 \big\}$
You are given that $\overline{x}=11$ and $\overline{y}=2$. Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places." :question/worked-solution "The linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the data sets

$$
x=\big\{x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}
$$

and

$$
y=\big\{y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}
$$

is given by

$$
\rho(x,y) = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))(y_{i} - y^(―)) \\
&= (13 - 11)(-1 - 2) + (10 - 11)(3 - 2) \\
&= + (9 - 11)(2 - 2) + (12 - 11)(4 - 2) \\
&= (2)(-3) + (-1)(1) + (-2)(0) + (1)(2) \\
&=-6 - 1 + 0 + 2 \\
&=-5
\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
S_{xx} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2} \\
&= (13 - 11)^{2} + (10 - 11)^{2} + (9 - 11)^{2} + (12 - 11)^{2} \\
&= 4 + 1 + 4 + 1 \\
&= 10 \\
S_{yy} &= ∑_(i = 1)^(n)(y_{i} - y^(―))^{2} \\
&= (-1 - 2)^{2} + (3 - 2)^{2} + (2 - 2)^{2} + (4 - 2)^{2} \\
&= 9 + 1 + 0 + 4 \\
&= 14
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ρ(x, y) &= ((-5))/(\sqrt{10} \cdot \sqrt{14}) \\
&\approx - \frac{5}{3.162278 \cdot 3.741657} \\
&\approx - 0.42
\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places."} {:db/id 17592186050406} {:db/id 17592186097074 :question/id #uuid "28ac07ed-0352-5aec-af24-65f8f8be76d3" :question/math-academy-id "q-134189"} {:db/id 17592186097077 :question/id #uuid "14a0c795-8e3a-5c60-8b7a-a39ebad5bd0d" :question/math-academy-id "q-134206"} {:db/id 17592186049206 :topic/encompasses [{:db/id 17592186428837 :encompassing/rationale "Initial Codex estimate from captured target-band crossing frequency. $$

- If $\mid \rho \mid \lt 0.3$, then the correlation is **negligible.** There is no (linear) correlation.![](images/9a/9afa80bfadc40b8b832b17dcea10d66d5a08955909d5bea66c7c010558b5ea19.png)" 17592186097695 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097891 :tutorial/content "Suppose we have data sets

$$
x=\big\{x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}
$$

and

$$
y=\big\{y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}
$$

of the same size.

Let's now introduce the following notation:

$$
S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, \qquad S_{yy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\overline{y})^2, \qquad S_{xy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Notice that $S_{xx}, S_{yy}$, and $S_{xy}$ are the sums of square deviations found in the formulas for the variance of $x$, the variance of $y$, and covariance of $x$ and $y$, respectively.

Using the previous definition, we can show that the correlation coefficient can be calculated as follows:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}\,
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1ab8695a-49cb-5bc1-8934-ffd2ff28261e" :tutorial/math-academy-id 5966 :tutorial/title "The Linear Correlation Coefficient in Sigma Notation"} :step/id #uuid "2e0466e2-c1f8-573f-bdcb-205404d8cec2" :step/math-academy-id 36415 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097694}} {:db/id 17592186097717 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097902 :tutorial/content "To calculate $\rho$, we use the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ρ(x, y) &= (Cov(x, y))/(σ_{x} \cdot σ_{y})
\end{aligned}
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance between $x$ and $y$, and
- $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations of $x$ and $y$, respectively.

For example, consider data sets $x$ and $y$ such that

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y)=-9, \qquad \sigma_x=6, \qquad \sigma_y=2
$$

Substituting our numbers into the formula above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
ρ(x, y) &= ((-9))/((6) \cdot (2)) \\
&= ((-9))/(12) \\
&=-0.75
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mid \rho \mid \gt 0.7$, the correlation is strong. Also, since $\rho$ is negative, the correlation is negative.

Therefore, there is a strong negative correlation between $x$ and $y$." :tutorial/id #uuid "6f296964-c1ff-5379-861d-1a9809ca7cc6" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6586 :tutorial/title "Calculating the Correlation Coefficient"} :step/id #uuid "c58771bb-e2f1-5f3c-9354-320e7568cc2d" :step/math-academy-id 39739 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097606}} {:db/id 17592186097718 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097903 :tutorial/content "Let's derive the following result:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
$$

We start with the definition of the correlation coefficient $\rho$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
ρ &= (Cov(x, y))/(σ_{x} \cdot σ_{y})
\end{aligned}
$$

We have

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = \dfrac1n \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}) = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{n}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}
σ_{x} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)(x_{i} - x^(―))^{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{S_{xx}}{n}} \\
σ_{y} &= \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}∑_(i = 1)^(n)(y_{i} - y^(―))^{2}} = \sqrt{\frac{S_{yy}}{n}}
\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our definition for $\rho$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
ρ &= (Cov(x, y))/(σ_{x} \cdot σ_{y}) \\
&= ((\frac{S_{xy}}{n}))/(\sqrt{\frac{S_{xx}}{n}} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{S_{yy}}{n}}) \\
&= ((\frac{S_{xy}}{n}))/(\sqrt{\frac{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}{n^{2}}}) \\
&= ((\frac{S_{xy}}{n}))/((\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}{n})) \\
&= ((\frac{S_{xy}}{n}))/((\frac{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}{n})) \\
&= \frac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "219dd7c3-97f9-5504-ad97-d8710a6cf5bc" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6587 :tutorial/title "Proving the Formula for Rho in Terms of Squared Deviations"} :step/id #uuid "be8ab20d-d46f-516f-aba3-1048baeb14b1" :step/math-academy-id 39740}] :activity/title "The Linear Correlation Coefficient" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186096858} {:db/id 17592186097603 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097862 :tutorial/content "The **linear correlation coefficient,** denoted $\rho$ (the Greek letter "rho"), is a number that gives the strength of the *linear* dependence between two sets of paired observations $(x,y)$.

$y$-axis." :question/worked-solution "Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$"} {:db/id 17592186233120 :question/id #uuid "73d11496-6181-52ca-9d4d-b27d18c44afc" :question/math-academy-id "q-10878"} {:db/id "978ac109-c615-5055-9e0a-f164ca3a1990" :step/math-academy-id 22383 :step/next {:db/id 17592186093329}} {:db/id 17592186093327 :step/content {:db/id 17592186093442 :tutorial/content "The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50c999b-ac30-5116-acbd-795f13cc2b3d" :knowledge-point/title "Determining the Intercepts of a Normal Line"} :step/id #uuid "434b8ac4-0cfe-5365-987b-8d6de7b04e04" :step/math-academy-id 671} {:db/id 17592186093442 :tutorial/content "The equation of the normal line to the curve $y = f(x)$ at the point $P(x_1,y_1),$ in point-slope form, is given by

$$
y - y_1 = m (x - x_1), \hspace{1cm} m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}.
$$

Here, $m=-\dfrac{1}{f'(x_1)}$ because the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line, and $f'(x_1)$ represents the slope of the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ at the point $(x_1,y_1).$

For example, suppose we want to compute the equation of the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $A(1,1).$ This normal line is the dashed line shown below, which is perpendicular to the solid tangent line. 

![](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Since $y=x^2,$ we have $f(x)=x^2.$ We begin by calculating the derivative of $f(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
f'(x) 		 = \dfrac {\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(x^2)= 2x
$$

At $A(1,1),$ the slope of the tangent line is given by

$$
f'(1) 	= 2(1) = 2.
$$

However, we want the normal line, and the slope of the normal line is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the tangent line:

$$
m = -\dfrac{1}{f'(1)} = -\dfrac{1}{2}
$$

 

Finally, we work out the equation of the normal line using the point-slope form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-1 & =-\frac{1}{2}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{1}{2}+1 \\ y & =-\frac{x}{2}+\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of the normal line is $y=-\dfrac x 2 + \dfrac 3 2.$ We could also write this in standard form as $x+2y=3.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "c50c999b-ac30-5116-acbd-795f13cc2b3d" "![](images/7a/7abc70a954ec2bb29c909f92b5a88655f8f3c66270ca0947487a8bc5f5e4deda.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $2\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $24\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $12\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{8}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $4\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=12\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=12I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{8}}=8q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=4\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
24=12I+8q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(24) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12I+8q+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =12\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8\,\frac{dq}{dt}+4\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\,\frac{dI}{dt}+2I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $2\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=6-3I-2q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=2$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =6-3I(0)-2q(0) \\  & =6-3\cdot 2-2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =-1,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=2$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =A{e}^{-0}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 2 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-A{e}^{-t}-2B{e}^{-2t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-1$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =-A{e}^{-0}-2B{e}^{-0} \\ -1 & =-A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2 &=A+B \\ -1 &=-A-2B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=3$ and $B=-1.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-2t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186372925 :question/id #uuid "ec7eedce-fc35-5301-816a-4bb7cc4477d9" :question/math-academy-id "q-345230" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186231408 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "c6faa97d-4d8e-5d67-bb99-8aae6de5a840" :knowledge-point/title "Solving an Equation Governing the Current in an RCL Circuit: Constant EMF"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "e35d4f95-5cc9-5b1e-948f-3f8ad0b14282" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "I(t)=2{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-3t/2}" :db/id 17592186372927} {:answer/id #uuid "d707e33c-e0a0-557c-9b4b-002604e3e4d9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "I(t)=2{e}^{-3t/2}+{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186372928} {:answer/id #uuid "10b84a1a-1126-5e1b-a431-4ef4c7b12f9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "I(t)=2{e}^{-3t/2}-{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186372929} {:answer/id #uuid "c7754268-15f7-568c-a6e2-7efbca7c488b" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "I(t)=-{e}^{-3t/2}+2{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186372930} {:answer/id #uuid "a4acd14b-68f1-542b-bec8-cf4f2be4c069" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "I(t)={e}^{-3t/2}-2{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186372931}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "10b84a1a-1126-5e1b-a431-4ef4c7b12f9c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "I(t)=2{e}^{-3t/2}-{e}^{-t}" :db/id 17592186372929} :answer-field/id #uuid "c7592773-6af2-5116-b635-86d74e652343" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186372926}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/0b/0b6e5f0ccf9a4f34ad60e82306db85fce99816de088bf66c90fcaf1a5bac10ed.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $3\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $5\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $\frac{1}{3}\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=5\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=5I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{\frac{1}{3}}=3q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
3=5I+3q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(3) & =\frac{d}{dt}(5I+3q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+3\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+\frac{5}{2}\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{3}{2}I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t/2}$ and $I={e}^{-t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t/2}+B{e}^{-t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{2}{3}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}I-\frac{3}{2}q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=1$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}I(0)-\frac{3}{2}q(0) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}-\frac{5}{2}\cdot 1-\frac{3}{2}\cdot \frac{2}{3} \\  & =-2,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=1$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-3(0)/2}+B{e}^{-0} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3t/2}-B{e}^{-t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =-\frac{3}{2}A{e}^{-3(0)/2}-B{e}^{-0} \\ -2 & =-\frac{3}{2}A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}1 &=A+B \\ -2 &=-\frac{3}{2}A-B\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $A=2$ and $B=-1.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=2{e}^{-3t/2}-{e}^{-t}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186372932 :question/id #uuid "c9acdec8-78fa-5121-85f5-7da3b379926b" :question/math-academy-id "q-345231"} {:db/id 17592186499467 :question/id #uuid 17592186045487 :db/ident :question.difficulty/moderate} :question/problem "![](images/53/5322f43ff1eeee6e06b3c393cc1b59c9af32bc2e7dba66766607af117954ace1.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*" :question/worked-solution "The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $20\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.1\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $10\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=20\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=20I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.1}=10q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=10\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)=20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(8\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(20I+10q+10\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -8\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =20\,\frac{dI}{dt}+10\,\frac{dq}{dt}+10\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t))+2(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(t)) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) \\ (2\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)+(-2\alpha )\operatorname{sin}⁡(t) & =-\frac{4}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}2\beta &=0\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)) \\ -2\alpha &=-\frac{4}{5}\, && (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(t))\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{2}{5}$ and $\beta =0.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186385934 :question/id #uuid "dd487be7-9e9e-5c43-b82c-f04901db73d5" :question/math-academy-id "q-345412"} {:db/id 17592186499542 :question/id #uuid :topic/math-academy-id 6726} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186231792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231991 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will use Kirchhoff's voltage law to derive a second-order differential equation that governs the current $I(t)$ in an RCL circuit.

![](images/d1/d1ce9424aca366d9028319fa2035e01339b26963e39150a8b14b8f2b34d67138.png)

In a series RCL circuit, Kirchhoff's voltage law states that the source voltage equals the sum of the voltage drops:

$$
E(t)=V_R+V_C+V_L
$$

For the three components:

- Resistor: the voltage drop is proportional to the current,

$$
V_R=RI.
$$

- Capacitor: the charge $q$ and capacitor voltage satisfy $q=CV_C,$ so

$$
V_C=\dfrac{q}{C}.
$$

- Inductor: the voltage drop is proportional to the rate of change of current,

$$
V_L=L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

Substituting these into Kirchhoff's voltage law gives

$$
E=RI+\dfrac{q}{C}+L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

To obtain a differential equation in terms of $I$ only, we first differentiate both sides with respect to $t{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(E) & =\frac{d}{dt}(RI+\frac{q}{C}+L\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ \frac{dE}{dt} & =R\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{1}{C}\cdot \frac{dq}{dt}+L\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that the current $I(t),$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q(t),$ measured in coulombs:

$$
I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Since $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}=I,$ we get the second-order differential equation governing the current:

$$
L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+R\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+\dfrac{1}{C}I=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Finally, dividing both sides by $L$ gives an equivalent form:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+\dfrac{R}{L}\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+\dfrac{1}{LC}I=\dfrac{1}{L} \cdot \dfrac{\mathrm{d}E}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Let's see a more concrete derivation in the next example." :tutorial/id #uuid "e9875681-c31f-535a-b3e2-7fcec32a16e3" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14791 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid 17592186231994 :tutorial/content "When we solve a second-order differential equation for the current $I(t),$ we often write the solution in the form

$$
I(t)=I_c(t)+I_p(t),
$$

where

- $I_c(t)$ is the **transient current**, which decays to $0$ as $t\to\infty,$ and

- $I_p(t)$ is the **steady-state current**, which governs the current’s long-term behavior.

To determine a unique solution for $I(t),$ we must specify two initial conditions, typically $I(0)$ and $I'(0).$

The current is often given directly as an initial condition, for example, $I(0)=I_0.$ We are also often given the initial *capacitor charge*, $q(0)=q_0.$

To find the other condition $I'(0),$ we use Kirchhoff's voltage law equation:

$$
E(t) = RI+\dfrac{q}{C}+L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Solving for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{1}{L}E - \dfrac{R}{L}I - \dfrac{q}{LC}.
$$

Now evaluate at $t=0{:}$

$$
I'(0) = \dfrac{1}{L}E(0) - \dfrac{R}{L}I(0) - \dfrac{1}{LC}q(0)
$$

So, if the initial charge $q(0)$ and initial current $I(0)$ are given, we can compute $I'(0)$ by substituting those values into the formula above.

In the next slide, we'll determine the initial conditions of a differential equation that governs the current in a given circuit." :tutorial/id #uuid "a6f06e46-ed1e-5e49-a9f8-679033a08a0f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14808 :tutorial/title "Initial Conditions for Solving the ODE Governing the Current in an RCL Circuit"} :step/id #uuid "10bd959b-3db6-58ef-8e40-eabd05f87aab" :step/math-academy-id 603155 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231820}} {:db/id 17592186231820 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232020 :tutorial/content "Suppose a circuit with a constant EMF of $E=8\,\textrm{V},$ resistance of $R=6\,\Omega,$ capacitance of $C=0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and inductance of $L=2\,\textrm{H},$ satisfies Kirchhoff's voltage law equation

$$
8=6I+4q+2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

First, let's derive the differential equation for $I$ by differentiating both sides with respect to $t{:}$

$$
0=6\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}+2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}.
$$

Since $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}=I,$ the differential equation for $I$ is

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+3\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+2I=0.
$$

Now suppose the initial charge and current are $q(0)=\dfrac12$ and $I(0)=1,$ respectively. Solving our first relation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = 4-3I-2q.
$$

Then, the initial conditions for the current we use to solve the ODE are $I(0)=1$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =4-3I(0)-2q(0) \\  & =4-3\cdot 1-2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the resulting initial value problem

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+3\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+2I=0, \qquad I(0) = 1, \quad I'(0) = 0,
$$

we obtain

$$
I(t)=2e^{-t}-e^{-2t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02b0c1dd-4819-5337-bc05-870ded85d834" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14901 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "a6ed1a27-61c7-514f-ab23-a91a7edba38d" :step/math-academy-id 608077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231794}}] :activity/title "Modeling Current in RCL Circuits With Second-Order ODEs" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186231523} {:db/id 17592186231792 :step/content {:db/id 17592186231991 :tutorial/content "In this lesson, we will use Kirchhoff's voltage law to derive a second-order differential equation that governs the current $I(t)$ in an RCL circuit.

the Current in an RCL Circuit: Sinusoidal EMF"} :step/id #uuid "dfab021e-6bf7-5ab4-8bd9-2af9f811ab5b" :step/math-academy-id 602729} {:db/id 17592186231994 :tutorial/content "When we solve a second-order differential equation for the current $I(t),$ we often write the solution in the form

$$
I(t)=I_c(t)+I_p(t),
$$

where

- $I_c(t)$ is the **transient current**, which decays to $0$ as $t\to\infty,$ and

- $I_p(t)$ is the **steady-state current**, which governs the current’s long-term behavior.

To determine a unique solution for $I(t),$ we must specify two initial conditions, typically $I(0)$ and $I'(0).$

The current is often given directly as an initial condition, for example, $I(0)=I_0.$ We are also often given the initial *capacitor charge*, $q(0)=q_0.$

To find the other condition $I'(0),$ we use Kirchhoff's voltage law equation:

$$
E(t) = RI+\dfrac{q}{C}+L\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}
$$

Solving for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$ gives

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = \dfrac{1}{L}E - \dfrac{R}{L}I - \dfrac{q}{LC}.
$$

Now evaluate at $t=0{:}$

$$
I'(0) = \dfrac{1}{L}E(0) - \dfrac{R}{L}I(0) - \dfrac{1}{LC}q(0)
$$

So, if the initial charge $q(0)$ and initial current $I(0)$ are given, we can compute $I'(0)$ by substituting those values into the formula above.

In the next slide, we'll determine the initial conditions of a differential equation that governs the current in a given circuit." :tutorial/id #uuid "a6f06e46-ed1e-5e49-a9f8-679033a08a0f" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14808 :tutorial/title "Initial Conditions for Solving the ODE Governing the Current in an RCL Circuit"} {:db/id 17592186231820 :step/content {:db/id 17592186232020 :tutorial/content "Suppose a circuit with a constant EMF of $E=8\,\textrm{V},$ resistance of $R=6\,\Omega,$ capacitance of $C=0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and inductance of $L=2\,\textrm{H},$ satisfies Kirchhoff's voltage law equation

$$
8=6I+4q+2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}.
$$

First, let's derive the differential equation for $I$ by differentiating both sides with respect to $t{:}$

$$
0=6\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}+2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}.
$$

Since $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}=I,$ the differential equation for $I$ is

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+3\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+2I=0.
$$

Now suppose the initial charge and current are $q(0)=\dfrac12$ and $I(0)=1,$ respectively. Solving our first relation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = 4-3I-2q.
$$

Then, the initial conditions for the current we use to solve the ODE are $I(0)=1$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =4-3I(0)-2q(0) \\  & =4-3\cdot 1-2\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the resulting initial value problem

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2I}{\mathrm{d}t^2}+3\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}+2I=0, \qquad I(0) = 1, \quad I'(0) = 0,
$$

we obtain

$$
I(t)=2e^{-t}-e^{-2t}.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "02b0c1dd-4819-5337-bc05-870ded85d834" :tutorial/math-academy-id 14901 :tutorial/title "A Worked Example"} :step/id #uuid "a6ed1a27-61c7-514f-ab23-a91a7edba38d" :step/math-academy-id 608077 :step/next {:db/id 17592186231794}} {:db/id 17592186232020 :tutorial/content "Suppose a circuit with a constant EMF of $E=8\,\textrm{V},$ resistance of $R=6\,\Omega,$ capacitance of $C=0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and inductance of $L=2\,\textrm{H},$ satisfies Kirchhoff's voltage law equation

$$

Now suppose the initial charge and current are $q(0)=\dfrac12$ and $I(0)=1,$ respectively. Solving our first relation for $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t},$ we have

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186097496 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097924 :tutorial/content "An **exponential function** is a function where a variable is contained within an exponent. For example, the function below is an exponential function:

$$
f(x) = 3^x
$$

Just like any other function, we can evaluate it for some particular value of $x,$ say at $x={\color{blue}{4}},$ by substituting this value of $x$ into the function:

$$
f(4) = 3^{\color{blue}{4}} = 81
$$

Another example of an exponential function is $g(x)$ below:

$$
g(x) = 16\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x
$$

We can evaluate this function at $x={\color{blue}{4}}$ using the power of quotient rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(4) & =16\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{4} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{{1}^{4}}{{2}^{4}} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{1}{16} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Exponential functions are of huge practical importance in science, engineering, economics, and many other disciplines. Let's practice evaluating them." :tutorial/id #uuid "155b9a63-2c55-5f26-a41f-b777e7afa911" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8843 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "28a95194-58c2-5aab-b5ec-1edc7f9c4953" :step/math-academy-id 166109 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097497}} {:db/id 17592186097497 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096657 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096390 :question/id #uuid "d03736b3-a7d8-52b3-894d-4ce2d04ee31c" :question/math-academy-id "e-14257"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "9283940a-cad8-51b5-b8c2-dc42ad8de264" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048652} {:db/id 17592186048683}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097195} {:db/id 17592186097242} {:db/id 17592186097323} {:db/id 17592186488193}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating an Exponential Function"} :step/id #uuid "e368b5da-f79a-5928-9c93-43f4a0dee7a5" :step/math-academy-id 166110 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097498}} {:db/id 17592186097498 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096658 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096391 :question/id #uuid "a83c1301-18cf-5622-8a4a-73f9d18e36b8" :question/math-academy-id "e-14260"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "6bab04f2-5e9a-55e7-9669-63e15938be0a" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186096957} {:db/id 17592186097202} {:db/id 17592186097243} {:db/id 17592186488187} {:db/id 17592186488251} {:db/id 17592186508914} {:db/id 17592186508982}] :knowledge-point/title "Evaluating a Function in a Modeling Problem"} :step/id #uuid "103957a3-310c-54ce-8227-8f216b6f4683" :step/math-academy-id 166114 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097499}} {:db/id 17592186097499 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097925 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the following exponential function:

$$
f(t) = C\cdot 4^t
$$

In addition, we're told that $f(3) = 128.$ Can we use this information to find the unknown constant $C?$

To solve this problem, we substitute $t=3$ and $f(t) = 128$ and solve for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}128 & =C\cdot {4}^{3} \\ 128 & =C\cdot 64 \\ \frac{128}{64} & =C \\ 2 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $C=2.$ So our function expressed in full is

$$
f(t) = 2\cdot 4^t.
$$

We sometimes say that the **initial value** of the function is $2,$ because if we evaluate $f$ at $t=0,$ we get

$$
f(0) = 2\cdot 4^0 = 2\cdot 1 = 2.
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "6820cdab-7e0a-5a90-adb1-880e4eb4a8de" :tutorial/math-academy-id 8846 :tutorial/title "Solving for an Unknown Constant"} :step/id #uuid "0d53b42c-c931-5e58-b073-7217b0bb9ac4" :step/math-academy-id 166118 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097500}} {:db/id 17592186097500 :step/content {:db/id 17592186096659 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186096392 :question/id #uuid "ca8cd4d6-8136-59bb-a033-6ba9ae8c06ed" :question/math-academy-id "e-14262"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "b0cee2b0-6cc8-5281-8ea2-02400b2980e1" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186050613}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186097196} {:db/id 17592186097322} {:db/id 17592186488261} {:db/id 17592186488265} {:db/id 17592186508929}] :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Initial Value"} :step/id #uuid "546da0c9-4c8f-57c2-9e29-200dc3ee9f2d" :step/math-academy-id 166119 :step/next {:db/id 17592186097501}} {:db/id 17592186097501 :step/content {:db/id 17592186097926 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following exponential function:

First, we use the fact that $h(x)=64$ to write our equation as

plane $x-y+z=1$ and the cylinder ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to find the minimum value of 

$$
f(x,y,z)=2x-2y+z
$$

subject to the constraints 

$$
g(x,y,z)=x-y+z=1,\,h(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2.
$$

Since $f(x,y,z)$ is continuous and the constraint is closed and bounded, $f(x,y,z)$ reaches a global maximum and a global minimum on the constraint. 

Therefore, by the method of Lagrange multipliers, we must solve the following system:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) &=\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ g(x,y,z) &=1 \\ h(x,y,z) &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

We start by expanding the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\lambda ∇g(x,y,z)+\mu ∇h(x,y,z) \\ ⟨{f}_{x},{f}_{y},{f}_{z}⟩ & =\lambda ⟨{g}_{x},{g}_{y},{g}_{z}⟩+\mu ⟨{h}_{x},{h}_{y},{h}_{z}⟩ \\ ⟨2,-2,1⟩ & =\lambda ⟨1,-1,1⟩+\mu ⟨2x,2y,0⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following system:

$$
\begin{aligned}\left\{\begin{aligned}2 &=\lambda +2\mu x \\ -2 &=-\lambda +2\mu y \\ 1 &=\lambda\end{aligned}\right.\,⇒\,\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ y &=-\frac{1}{2\mu } \\ \lambda &=1\end{aligned}\right.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mu $ can't be zero since this leads to a contradiction.

Next, we substitute our expressions for $x$ and $y$ into the second constraint:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & =2 \\ \frac{1}{4{\mu }^{2}}+\frac{1}{4{\mu }^{2}} & =2 \\ \frac{1}{2{\mu }^{2}} & =2 \\ {\mu }^{2} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \mu  & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

As a result, 

$$
x=\pm 1,\,y=∓1.
$$

Finally, we substitute $x$ and $y$ into the first constraint:

- If $x=1$ and $y=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+z & =1 \\ 1-(-1)+z & =1 \\ 2+z & =1 \\ z & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

- If $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y+z & =1 \\ -1-1+z & =1 \\ -2+z & =1 \\ z & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f$ has possible extreme values at the points

$$
(1,-1,-1),\,(-1,1,3).
$$

We evaluate $f$ at each of these points. These are given in the following table:

| $(x,y,z)$ | $(1,-1,-1)$ | $(-1,1,3)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y,z)$ | $3$ | $-1$ |

Therefore, the function reaches a minimum value at $(-1,1,3),$ and its minimum value is $-1.$"} {:db/id 17592186172385 :question/id #uuid "a33f04b0-b880-5f66-b37e-14b59e173b67" $$

$$

$$
